Docs, "Getting started": "Linear's GraphQL endpoint is: https://api.linear.app/graphql — It supports introspection so you can query the whole schema." The full schema SDL is also published in the official linear/linear repo at packages/sdk/src/schema.graphql (kept current by the repo's schema GitHub Action).

Docs, "Getting Started": "Our GraphQL API is explorable and queryable via Apollo Studio (studio.apollographql.com/public/Linear-API), no download or log in required. Click the Schema tab to browse the schema, and click the Explorer tab to run queries."

Docs, "Rate limiting" publishes exact per-auth limits ("API key — 2,500 requests per User per 1 hour; OAuth App — 5,000 per User; Unauthenticated — 600 per IP Address"), leaky-bucket refill, complexity limits, and response headers: "X-RateLimit-Requests-Limit — The maximum number of API requests you're permitted to make per hour."

Docs, "Deprecations": "Linear's GraphQL API doesn't have versioning like many REST APIs... we take breaking changes and deprecations seriously... If there's a noticeable breaking change in the API, we'll proactively reach out to developers that use that part of the API and give you plenty of time to make changes... We utilize the @deprecated directive to annotate deprecation warnings in the schema. In addition, changes to the API are listed with [API] prefix in the Linear changelog."

We've been using Linear for a couple months. It's kind of like Superhuman in that the primary benefit is hotkeys. Otherwise it is an issue tracker.
I just want to say the app is amazing and my team loves it. Good luck mitigating the DDoS, and even under attack, Linear is faster than JIRA.

I am so glad that I picked Linear for my startup. You folks have been consistently responsive, helpful, and keep delivering features that matter. It's been a delight after a decade of Jira and the gang.
I have used Linear on a couple of my hobby projects and it's a great tool to quickly capture features and bugs. My one gripe... is that the written copy fails to explain what the product actually is.

50ms user interactions is not what I would consider 'breathtakingly fast' as the website claims... I see lots of unnecessary animations that contribute massively to the perceived slowness of basic interactions.

Can't speak for other teams... but we migrated from JIRA to Linear for our small team, and haven't looked back. Just the simple fact that it feels like we can store and reference information from a ticket without spending 10 minutes waiting for it to load is a killer feature.

I stopped using Jira years ago... and work with one other full time person, making a complex software product, and I feel like I accomplish 2x as much as I used to with much more value, at far lower cost.

The killer missing feature for us is that we can't define different issue types... there's no way to show the issue layout as an expandable tree-view... Doesn't seem to be a way to add custom fields to different issue types.

Hell no. If you want jira, use Jira. Linear is better specifically because it's not Jira and doesn't try to be. A huge part of its appeal is that it actively prevents workflows like yours. On purpose.

I couldn't find a mention of it - but is there any plans or ability to self-host? I'm personally not a fan of keeping everything in the cloud... We unfortunately don't currently have plans to provide self-hosting.

After using Linear for a couple of months, one user said its main benefit is hotkeys, much like Superhuman. Otherwise it is just an issue tracker. They argued new trackers feel faster mainly because you leave the old backlog cruft behind, not because the tool fixes the organization's underlying problems.
After a few weeks of casual use: 'quite impressed. It's a definite improvement over Jira in simplicity and performance, but is missing quite a few features still. But still, it's my preference.'
Criticism of the restricted free plan, capped at 250 issues. Plenty of truly free options exist, so the user asked why Linear doesn't offer a free trial of an unrestricted plan instead.

Concern that Linear's privacy policy is generic and its Terms of Service grant Linear a license to use, reproduce and distribute posted content, including to other users. The commenter doesn't want discussion of security-critical bugs exposed that way.
'This is a `vi` of issue trackers. It's the kind of software which, after you use it, you desire whole web would use the same design philosophy.'
Uses Linear for a personal iOS side project and says it's 'so much fun to use compare to the JIRA I use at work all day.'

After 3 months at a new company, this user doesn't see much value over Jira, Trello, Asana or Monday. The command palette and fast UI are nice, but simple tasks like adding 2+ issues still take too many clicks or shortcuts. The Slack integration is 'non existent': you can't create issues from a conversation. Will keep using it but won't evangelize it.

Started using Linear a couple of weeks ago and the team is 'very happy', enjoying the speed and accessibility (desktop app, keyboard shortcuts). Complaint: desktop app update notifications come almost daily. The user now ignores the red dot, which actually signals unread inbox items.

A team that moved over early had previously used Pivotal Tracker, Jira, Trello, Asana and GitHub. They found Linear 'by far the most polished, productive interface.' Where Linear lacked granular configuration for their points/sprint workflow, they got most benefits using tags and other features. A former die-hard Pivotal Tracker user, they say going back is hard to imagine.

A paying customer for a month left Notion for lack of an API. Linear 'lacks some basic features,' but its GraphQL API and webhooks keep them happy. Their CI moves issues from staged to deployed and pushes associated HubSpot tickets to a customer success queue.
For a small team, Linear 'beats the hell out of JIRA.' They don't miss JIRA's 30+ second page loads, slow saves, confusing comments and accidental ticket body erasure on a heavily loaded instance.

A product/engineering manager of 10+ years calls Linear 'hands down the best tool I've used for ticketing.' They say it would be hard to work somewhere without it, and no other tool they use feels faster.
A small team migrated from JIRA to Linear and 'haven't looked back.' Being able to store and reference ticket information without waiting ages for it to load is 'a killer feature.'

A firmware team that uses JIRA heavily tried Linear and found key gaps:
- no custom issue types (Requirement/Bug/Signal) with hierarchies
- no expandable tree view, so requirements get flattened
- no per-type custom fields
- no Confluence equivalent
They also asked about a self-hosted version.

A team tried Linear for three months and found it fast, with all interactions instant, and great-looking. But it was 'quite complex. The information architecture is confusing.' They went back to GitHub Issues after spending too much time clicking and finding things.
'I love Linear,' but involving clients and external users for QA is a problem. Guest accounts, often temporary, are priced as full users, which makes it too expensive for them.

A triage team between Support and Engineering spends all day in Linear and loves it. Its biggest limitation is metadata: labels are lost when transferring issues to another team, or they clutter that team's labels. Workaround: they built tooling on the GraphQL API that records impact data as formatted comments and in their own database for metrics.
Used Linear on hobby projects and called it 'a great tool to quickly capture features and bugs.' Gripe: the new website copy fails to explain what the product actually is.

Happy customers who call it 'light and snappy, customisable just in the right amount,' with predictable UI/UX. Biggest weakness is workflow automation: even an email-to-ticket flow requires writing your own integration or going through Zapier.

Tried Linear for its performance claims and found it much better than Jira or Trello, but '50ms' isn't breathtakingly fast. Unnecessary animations add perceived slowness, and some aren't smooth (label menu color dots jiggle). Still, they called it much better than most alternatives on UI/performance.
